doc.title: Randy Brecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 12, 2022

chapter: Blood, Sweat & Tears and Horace Silver
title: Leaving for Horace Silver, Lew Soloff and the salaries
summary: He quit to play more, the band lost Al Kooper, he talked Lew Soloff into taking his seat, and BS&T pay soared while he made $147.50 a week.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: when Horace called. I really wanted to play. I only got to play one solo a night and it was mostly reading horn parts. And I thought I’d gotten enough out of it. And they were going to add a lead singer named David Clayton Thomas. They begged me to stay, they liked what I did, but I said — Al Kooper — we had a band meeting and he didn’t like the idea of adding another singer so he quit and at the same time I announced that I was going to join Horace Silver. My last words to them were: “I don’t think you guys will ever make it without Al Kooper.” And the tough part, and I’ll say this honestly, was after the record came out, their second record and it sold nine — no eleven million copies — it was number one for a year, won the Grammy of the year award, their salaries went up like 5,000 percent. I mean and I had to talk my friend Lew Soloff — it was funny, the day before I left I was doing a Joe Henderson big band rehearsal and Lewey was next to me and I explained the situation, I said, “Listen man, I need somebody to cover me or just take the gig, I’m leaving Blood, Sweat & Tears and it pays like a hundred dollars a week whether you work or don’t, it’s a salary.” And he didn’t really want to do it. In fact they had asked him previously. But by the end of the rehearsal I talked — “Look, they’re going to go in the studio” I just had him talked into doing it. So begrudgingly he took the gig. Two months later their salaries went up to like five thousand a week. I’m making two fifty a week with Horace.

You know you’re pushing a button with me because I was in a group that was fairly successfully locally and doing gigs, and the producer wanted us to get a lead singer who just stood there and sang — you know like a lead singer. And we just resisted the heck out of it. And the difference in the story was our salary never went up five thousand percent.

Yeah it was a funny time. And Lew and I would take trumpet lessons and had been doing that for a while with Edward Truetel in New Jersey. We’d take a bus to his house. Then Lewey started picking me up in a limo you know, cackling all the time. And like I said I was making two fifty a week and Horace had left out of the deal that he took taxes out. I’ll never forget these figures, so it was really $147.50 a week and I had to pay my hotel out of that.
